articles.title: La France et l’Allemagne veulent donner à l’Union le pouvoir de fermer son marché
articles.description:
Voilà pourquoi ce serait une petite révolution

L’article La France et l’Allemagne veulent donner à l’Union le pouvoir de fermer son marché est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent.
articles.content:
il y a 17 heures 
 
 
 
 Dans une lettre adressée le 5 octobre à la présidente de la Commission, accompagnée d’un non-paper de quatre pages, Emmanuel Macron et Friedrich Merz proposent de changer les règles du jeu commercial européen. 
 
 
 
 
 
 Temps de lecture:
 4 min
 
 

 

 

 
 
 
 

 


 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Date 
 
 
 5 octobre 2026 
 
 

 

 
 
 Partager 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 Abonnez-vous pour télécharger cet article en format PDF 
 
 
 →
 
 
 S'abonner 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
Aujourd’hui, le 5 octobre, le président français et le chancelier allemand ont adressé à la présidente de la Commission une lettre d’une page accompagnée d’un non-paper franco-allemand de trois pages. 

Ce format, qui n’engage formellement personne, est l’instrument habituel par lequel les deux capitales contribuent à fixer l’ordre du jour de la Commission. 

Il prolonge les discussions du Conseil européen des 18 et 19 juin, ainsi que celles du Conseil des ministres franco-allemand du 17 juillet, en vue du Conseil européen d’octobre.

Ces deux documents apportent plusieurs éléments nouveaux, alors que Paris et Berlin décrivent un « choc industriel massif » qui frappe des secteurs au cœur du modèle européen, de la pharmacie à l’automobile, en passant par l’aérospatiale, la machine-outil et la chimie.

Paris et Berlin demandent la mise en place d’un mécanisme de réponse systémique visant à réglementer l’accès au marché unique et à envisager un « blocage immédiat » à l’encontre de tout pays tiers qui tenterait d’entraver le rétablissement de conditions de concurrence équitables. Explicitement « country agnostic », ce mécanisme viserait à lutter contre toute forme de distorsion, « d’un produit isolé à un secteur entier, des subventions à la manipulation des devises ».

Son activation ne dépendrait pas d’un vote favorable des États membres, mais d’une majorité qualifiée inversée. La proposition de la Commission serait adoptée à moins qu’une majorité qualifiée ne s’y oppose pour que l’inertie joue en faveur de l’action, plutôt que contre celle-ci.

Sans attendre la mise en place de ce nouvel outil, les deux capitales appellent à une utilisation bien plus proactive des moyens existants. Elles souhaitent que la Commission lance davantage d’enquêtes de sa propre initiative, afin de veiller à ce que les États membres ayant déposé une plainte ne soient pas les seuls à subir le poids des représailles, qu’elle examine des secteurs entiers plutôt que des « catégories de produits restreintes » et enfin qu’elle déroge à la règle de la norme juridique la plus faible lorsque les intérêts de l’Union le justifient.

Le texte prévoit également que les niveaux sans précédent de non-conformité aux normes européennes, notamment en raison des « flux massifs de petits colis », entraînent des restrictions d’accès au marché unique. Une « loi sur l’accélération industrielle » et une « préférence européenne » ciblée dans les secteurs stratégiques devraient être adoptées d’ici fin 2026.

Paris et Berlin appellent enfin l’Eurogroupe, la BCE et la Commission à reprendre le dialogue avec les « autorités compétentes » sur les taux de change, un dialogue qui est au point mort depuis des années.

Aucun des deux textes ne nomme explicitement la Chine, mais le diagnostic désigne implicitement son économie en parlant de « surcapacités structurelles à l’échelle mondiale », de « subventions excessives et généralisées », de « manipulation monétaire », ou « flux massifs de petits colis » non conformes aux normes européennes.

Comme le fait remarquer Pascal Lamy, l’Union européenne a enregistré en 2025 un déficit commercial d’un milliard d’euros par jour avec la Chine. Les entreprises chinoises reçoivent trois à huit fois plus de soutien public que leurs concurrentes des pays de l’OCDE. À cela s’ajoute un yuan sous-évalué de 16 à 30 %, ainsi qu’une demande intérieure atrophiée, la consommation privée ne représentant que 40 % du PIB chinois, contre 53 % dans l’Union et 68 % aux États-Unis.

Le 8 octobre, le commissaire européen au Commerce et à la Sécurité économique, Maroš Šefčovič, coprésidera le groupe de travail « Commerce et Investissement » à Pékin avec son homologue Wang Wentao. Il a déclaré déclaré espérer revenir avec une « preuve de concept » abordant trois sujets : les hausses soudaines des exportations chinoises dans des secteurs industriels clefs, des moyens concrets d’accroître les exportations de produits européens vers la Chine, et une vision claire à long terme concernant les restrictions chinoises à l’exportation de matières premières, en particulier les terres rares.

La Commission a averti qu’en l’absence de « résultats tangibles », elle mettrait en œuvre ses instruments de défense commerciale. 

Les discussions qui auront lieu à Pékin cette semaine seront présentées au Conseil européen qui se réunira les 15 et 16 octobre.

articles.title: Au sein de l’AfD, on rêve d’annexer les Sudètes, une partie de l’Italie et l’Alsace-Lorraine
articles.description:
Nous cartographions les frontières révisionnistes de la « Grande Allemagne »

L’article Au sein de l’AfD, on rêve d’annexer les Sudètes, une partie de l’Italie et l’Alsace-Lorraine est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent.
articles.content:
il y a 18 heures 
 
 
 
 Nous cartographions les frontières de la « Grande Allemagne » des « territoires perdus » que certains cadres de l’extrême droite allemande rêvent désormais de reconquérir. 
 
 
 
 
 
 Temps de lecture:
 4 min
 
 

 

 

 
 
 
 

 


 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Date 
 
 
 5 octobre 2026 
 
 

 

 
 
 Partager 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 Abonnez-vous pour télécharger cet article en format PDF 
 
 
 →
 
 
 S'abonner 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
Des membres de l’Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), le parti d’extrême droite allemand, multiplient les « signaux irrédentistes » envers des régions ayant appartenu à l’espace germanophone, aujourd’hui situées dans d’autres pays européens. La démarche n’émane pas nécessairement de la direction du parti, mais aucune de ces prises de parole n’a pour autant fait l’objet de procédures disciplinaires à notre connaissance.

En 2018, le groupe AfD au Bundestag a interrogé le gouvernement sur le travail de la « référente culturelle pour la Prusse-Occidentale, la Posnanie, la Pologne centrale, la Volhynie et la Galicie », dans une série de questions où il réclame un financement institutionnel pour les associations d’expulsés.

En novembre 2019, Stephan Protschka, député de l’AfD au Bundestag, a participé au financement d’une stèle à Bytom rendant « hommage aux soldats allemands tombés pendant la Première et la Seconde Guerre mondiale, aux combattants des corps d’autodéfense et des corps francs, et aux Allemands de l’Est opprimés et assassinés ».

En 2024, Alice Weidel avait déclaré avoir toujours refusé d’utiliser le nom polonais, Głubczyce, de Leobschütz, la ville d’origine de la famille de son père, dans l’actuelle voïvodie d’Opole.

On remarque une accélération des provocations verbales en lien avec des « territoires perdus » depuis le début de l’année.

Après que l’État russe a classé en mai la Landsmannschaft Ostpreußen, une association culturelle des expulsés de Prusse-Orientale, comme « organisation indésirable », l’AfD a dénoncé cette décision et a demandé au gouvernement allemand s’il en avait discuté avec Moscou.

Le même mois, des élus de l’AfD en Bavière ont réclamé l’abrogation des décrets Beneš de 1945, qui ont servi de base légale à l’expulsion des Allemands des Sudètes de l’État tchécoslovaque reconstitué après sa dissolution par l’Allemagne nazie en 1938-1939. À l’occasion du congrès des Allemands des Sudètes, qui se tenait pour la première fois en Tchéquie, des membres de l’AfD ont défendu l’organisation de la manifestation malgré l’hostilité du parti tchèque d’extrême droite Liberté et démocratie directe (SPD), avec lequel l’AfD siège pourtant au Parlement européen dans le groupe Europe des nations souveraines (ESN).

Le 12 septembre, à Termeno, lors du congrès du mouvement de jeunesse du parti Süd-Tiroler Freiheit fondé par Eva Klotz, Jean-Pascal Hohm, le chef de l’organisation de jeunesse de l’AfD (Generation Deutschland), a repris le slogan du parti en déclarant : « Le Sud-Tyrol n’est pas l’Italie ».

L’Alsace, dont le territoire faisait partie du Saint-Empire romain germanique avant d’être rattaché à la France au XVIIe siècle, et qui a été annexée à deux reprises par l’Allemagne (en 1871 puis en 1940), a aussi fait l’objet de revendications.

Un jeune militant de Generation Deutschland, la jeunesse de l’AfD, Marco Eggebrecht, a publié sur X le 9 mai une photo de lui accompagnée de la phrase : « Comment je te regarde quand j’entends : l’Alsace-Lorraine doit redevenir une possession allemande ».

Trois jours plus tard, le député européen Tomasz Froelich, un membre de l’AfD élu en 2024, a attaqué la France et dénoncé « sa politique agressive d’assimilation linguistique », ainsi que « l’hypocrisie » de l’Union en raison de sa critique de la politique chinoise vis-à-vis des populations ouïghoures.

Im Elsass sprachen vor drei Generationen rund 90 Prozent der Bevölkerung Elsässisch – heute ist das eine aussterbende Sprache. Alles Folge der aggressiven sprachlichen Assimilationspolitik Frankreichs. Anstatt sich um den Schutz nationaler Minderheiten auf dem eigenen Kontinent… pic.twitter.com/Yp3g7mWxEj— Tomasz Froelich (@TomaszFroelich) May 12, 2026

Le 3 octobre, Jour de l’unité allemande, un dirigeant de Generation Deutschland, Luca Maurice Strauf, a décrit sur X la réunification comme « une victoire d’étape », en commentant une image qui inclut entre autres l’Alsace-Lorraine, le Luxembourg, l’Autriche mais pas la Silésie, la Poméranie et la Prusse-Orientale.

Der Vorstand der AfD-Jugend, Luca Maurice Strauf, mit völkischem Revisionismus zum Tag der deutschen Einheit. Der 3. Oktober für ihn nur ein "Etappen-Sieg" vor der "großdeutschen Lösung". Mittlerweile wieder gelöscht, aber das lässt tief blicken. pic.twitter.com/Hx4IrotVdN— Gareth Joswig (@garethmetik) October 3, 2026

Il a depuis supprimé sa publication.

articles.title: La Russie fait-elle face à une épidémie de peste ?
articles.description:
Ce que l’on sait sur le décès d’une femme le 2 octobre dans la région d’Irkoutsk

L’article La Russie fait-elle face à une épidémie de peste ? est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent.
articles.content:
il y a 1 jour 
 
 
 
 Depuis qu’une technicienne de laboratoire a brisé une éprouvette contenant ce qui pourrait être l'agent de la peste pulmonaire, plusieurs hôpitaux ont été placés sous quarantaine dans la région d'Irkoutsk.

Nous faisons le point sur ce que l'on sait à cette heure, et sur les implications d'une éventuelle propagation de l'infection. 
 
 
 
 
 
 Temps de lecture:
 5 min
 
 

 

 

 
 
 
 

 


 

 
 
 
 

 
Daria Chipilova, une technicienne de laboratoire russe de 28 ans, est morte dans la nuit du 1er au 2 octobre d’une pneumonie foudroyante dans la région sibérienne d’Irkoutsk. Elle travaillait à l’Institut « anti-peste » d’Irkoutsk, et les mesures de quarantaine prises depuis laissent penser que les autorités locales craignent un pathogène particulièrement contagieux.

Tout part de cet institut de recherche situé à Irkoutsk, qui est placé sous la tutelle du Rospotrebnadzor, le service fédéral de surveillance sanitaire.

Selon les médias locaux, Chipilova aurait brisé le 25 septembre une éprouvette contenant ce qui pourrait être l’agent de la peste pulmonaire. 

Il convient ainsi de rester prudent sur la piste de la peste. Le terme russe « protivochoumny » (« anti-peste ») vient de l’histoire de ce réseau d’instituts, qui étudie l’ensemble des « infections particulièrement dangereuses », et pas seulement la peste.

L’institut d’Irkoutsk disposerait d’un laboratoire dit « P3 », c’est-à-dire de niveau de biosécurité 3 sur une échelle de 4, dédié à l’étude des pathogènes dangereux. Un laboratoire P4 étant très coûteux, beaucoup d’instituts n’ont pas les moyens d’en construire un, même lorsque la nature des souches qu’ils manipulent le justifierait.

Alors que le protocole lui imposait de signaler l’incident, Chipilova n’en aurait parlé à personne et serait rentrée chez elle, laissant potentiellement au pathogène le temps de se propager.

Près de 200 personnes ont depuis été placées en quarantaine. Plusieurs hôpitaux de l’oblast ont pris des mesures préventives, tout comme l’usine d’aluminium de Chelekhov, principal employeur de la ville, qui a imposé le port du masque.

Si Chipilova avait donné l’alerte, elle aurait été immédiatement isolée et placée sous antibiotiques à titre préventif, ce qui aurait très probablement suffi à enrayer l’infection et à empêcher toute contamination.

Les instituts de recherche qui travaillent sur des pathogènes dangereux appliquent des procédures strictes, car les accidents arrivent. Mais l’immense majorité d’entre eux est rapidement prise en charge, et n’a que des conséquences limitées.

La souche à l’origine de la mort de Chipilova semble particulièrement virulente, et il est donc possible que la « fenêtre de tir » pour administrer un antibiotique ait été très resserrée. Qu’elle soit morte malgré son hospitalisation dès le 29 septembre ne signifie pas pour autant que la souche résiste aux antibiotiques. Or tout dépend de ce point : si la souche est sensible, les personnes placées en quarantaine pourront être traitées préventivement.

Mais si cette souche résiste à de nombreux antibiotiques et s’avère difficile à traiter, les autorités seront contraintes d’étendre leurs mesures de précaution et de quarantaine.

Chipilova elle-même, une fois hospitalisée, à avoué avoir brisé la fiole et a potentiellement livré bien plus de détails sur la fiole et sur l’incident aux autorités 

Les autorités sanitaires ont en principe pu effectuer des prélèvements sur Chipilova et séquencer la bactérie responsable de l’infection. Elles connaissent donc probablement déjà le profil exact de la souche à l’origine de sa mort.

Ce séquençage donne de fortes indications sur sa virulence et sur la présence éventuelle de gènes de résistance aux antibiotiques. Cette résistance peut ensuite être confirmée en mettant en culture les bactéries prélevées pour tester directement sur elles l’ensemble des antibiotiques.

Il est donc fort probable que les autorités russes en sachent déjà bien davantage que ce qui circule dans les médias.

Sous l’URSS, les instituts de recherche sur les maladies infectieuses étaient chargés d’étudier les pathogènes naturels et d’apprendre à les combattre, mais aussi, le cas échéant, de transmettre au programme Biopreparat toute souche naturelle jugée particulièrement « intéressante ». Quand bien même l’institut d’Irkoutsk n’aurait plus aucun lien avec un programme d’armes biologiques, on ignore quelles souches y sont conservées, et il n’est pas exclu qu’il ait gardé des souches issues de ce programme soviétique.

Un point crucial reste flou à ce stade : la nature exacte du pathogène.

Daria Chipilova ayant tout dit de l’incident une fois hospitalisée, elle aurait donc potentiellement informé les autorités de la nature de la bactérie en cause mais aussi de ses déplacements depuis le 25 septembre.

À partir de là, deux données sont essentielles pour les autorités sanitaires : la vitesse à laquelle l’infection peut se propager, et la sensibilité de cette souche aux antibiotiques.

Aucun autre cas n’est confirmé à ce stade, mais si une chaîne de transmission s’est installée, elle peut très vite devenir impossible à contenir, le nombre de personnes à placer en quarantaine croissant alors de façon exponentielle.

L’autre donnée essentielle est de savoir si cette souche est sensible aux antibiotiques, et le cas échéant auxquels. C’est ici que le spectre d’une vieille souche d’arme biologique soviétique prendrait toute sa gravité.

Une arme biologique peut avoir été rendue insensible aux antibiotiques courants, à l’exception d’un ou deux que l’URSS pensait être seule à détenir.

Il paraît en revanche peu probable qu’on cherche à créer un agent contre lequel il n’existerait aucun remède, précisément parce que ce type d’accident arrive.

Même en écartant l’hypothèse de la souche soviétique, qu’aucun élément n’étaye à ce stade mais que l’histoire de cet institut oblige à considérer, il reste un nombre croissant de souches parfaitement naturelles et de plus en plus résistantes aux antibiotiques.

La montée de l’antibiorésistance est devenue un enjeu majeur de santé publique.

articles.title: ‘Nearly all women arriving on small boats have been raped,’ UK Home Secretary admits
articles.description:
UK Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood revealed that nearly all women crossing from France to Britain in small boats have likely faced rape during their journey.

Source
articles.content:
Nearly every woman waiting in northern France to cross to Britain in a small boat has probably been raped on the journey, the UK Home Secretary has said.
Shabana Mahmood made the claim in an interview with The Rest Is Politics: Leading, the podcast hosted by the former Conservative minister Rory Stewart and Alastair Campbell, Tony Blair’s former adviser.
“We’re not in control of this border,” she admitted.
“The sifting of the people that end up in the north of France and are about to get on a dinghy is done by criminal gangs who are also, by the way, people traffickers. You can almost guarantee that every woman that’s in the north of France has probably been raped along the journey. Some of the men too, they’ve certainly been abused and threatened.”
That, she said, “is not the model that should decide whether somebody gets to come to the UK, make this their place of sanctuary and ultimately become one of us.”
In the same interview she turned on the demonstrators who have praised her border policy, telling them to “sod off” and saying they would want to drive her out of her own country because she is a Muslim.
No Home Office assessment quantifying sexual violence on the routes into northern France has been released alongside Mahmood’s interview.
Home Office statistics record the sex, age and nationality of those detected on arrival, not what happened to them before they embarked.
Women are a minority of those who do arrive. A House of Commons Library briefing, drawing on Home Office data, put detected small-boat arrivals at about 33,000 in the year to June 2026, of whom roughly 13 per cent were adult women, 72 per cent adult men and 15 per cent children.
The department’s own figure for that period was 33,374, down 23 per cent on the 43,309 recorded a year earlier. Eritreans, Sudanese, Afghans, Somalis and Iranians made up two-thirds of the total.
Women who land are held at short-term sites such as Manston, in Kent, southeast England, where the Home Office handed out 974 hijabs in the first six months of the year, Brussels Signal reported.
Imran Hussain, of the Refugee Council, welcomed the recognition that women and girls face sexual violence in the conflicts they flee and on the journeys that follow, and used the remarks to argue for wider safe routes than the sponsorship scheme the government has announced.
Mahmood said in June she would open new legal routes for what she called genuine refugees while closing loopholes that had been abused. The first of them, allowing communities and universities to sponsor arrivals, is due to open from this autumn.
The remarks come as opposition to the crossings has moved from the ballot box to the quayside.
On the weekend of September 5 and 6, men in black and balaclavas, linked to a group calling itself Patriot Platform, blocked roads at Dover and clashed with police in Portsmouth after about 140 people were landed at Eastney.
The group is run by Daniel Thomas, an associate of Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, the activist better known as Tommy Robinson, according to the campaign group Hope Not Hate.
Mahmood told chief constables on September 10 the scenes carried “obvious malign intent” and urged them to use their powers to ban face coverings.
The tactic has not stopped.
On September 22 hundreds gathered at a marina in Gosport, Hampshire, southern England, to meet a dinghy carrying 51 people. The boat was diverted and docked at Dover instead after 33 hours at sea, and six people were arrested.
Hampshire’s police and crime commissioner, Donna Jones, said the two operations had cost more than £250,000 (€287,000) and that she expected more to come.
On October 4, about 150 demonstrators gathered at a marina in Gosport as the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI) brought ashore 149 people picked up in mid-Channel.
Flares were let off, police vans were blocked and there were scuffles. Hampshire Police had already prohibited face coverings. Twelve people were arrested, including on suspicion of assaulting officers, affray and racially aggravated public order.

A French charity that works with migrants on the Channel coast has been accused of helping to put children onto small boats bound for Britain, after video filmed near Boulogne-sur-Mer, northern France, was published by the online outlet Voxpopuli. https://t.co/mrGAiSHVbw
— Brussels Signal (@brusselssignal) September 28, 2026

articles.title: Key witness in Bardella anti-Semitism case says Mediapart manipulated his words
articles.description:
In a recent interview, key witness Laurent G. accused Mediapart of manipulating and distorting his words regarding Rassemblement National president Jordan Bardella's views and statements.

Source
articles.content:
A key witness cited by Mediapart in its investigation of Rassemblement National (RN) president Jordan Bardella has said the outlet manipulated him, distorted some of his remarks and invented others.
Laurent G., a former official of the Front National de la Jeunesse (FNJ) in Seine-Saint-Denis, north of Paris, spoke on October 5 to Éric Morillot on Les Incorrectibles, on condition of anonymity.
Clips were first shown on CNews. Asked at the end of the interview whether he had been manipulated, he replied: “Yes, I was manipulated by Mediapart, which distorted my remarks.”
He said he had decided to speak for three reasons: To state publicly that his words had been distorted and to explain why; to rebut rumours that he was trying to destabilise the Rassemblement National’s campaign, which he called “totally false”; and to say that he bore no ill will towards Bardella or Marine Le Pen and supported both in the campaign now under way.
Laurent G. said he met Bardella at the end of 2013, when he himself no longer held any responsibility in the Front National (FN), although he still attended events at the Seine-Saint-Denis federation, including the party’s youth forum.
Bardella, he said, was at the start of his militant career; his own was over.
They crossed paths “perhaps four or five times”. The relationship was “courteous” and militant, not personal.
“We were not close, even if I have esteem for him, and we are not friends.”
He said they never spoke by telephone, that he did not think he had ever had Bardella’s number, and that Bardella never replied to his emails.
The sharpest dispute concerns Eustace Mullins’ book The Secrets of the Federal Reserve.
Mediapart reported that Laurent G. had described the book as Bardella’s “bedside book”.
He told Morillot: “I never said to Mediapart that Mr Jordan Bardella had [that book] as a bedside book. I never said it.”
Pressed, he called the phrase not a distortion but “invented remarks”.
What he said he had told the journalist was that Bardella had made a good impression — well turned-out, energetic, with “great intellectual curiosity” and already solid knowledge — and that, over pizza after a youth-forum evening, there had been a brief discussion of the book, a publishing success in patriotic circles two or three years earlier.
Bardella, he said, merely knew the contents. He had mentioned it to illustrate curiosity, not devotion.
He also rejected a passage in which Mediapart quoted him as recalling that Bardella “took an interest in the theories about the possible survival of Adolf Hitler after the Second World War”.
He said he had not said that.
The exchange, again at the pizza dinner, concerned a single item Bardella had seen online, presented as drawn from declassified FBI documents and raising the possibility that Hitler had fled to South America.
Laurent G. said he had replied that he did not really believe it, and that it was “a reaction of intellectual curiosity to one plausible piece of information”, not an interest in such theories in general.
“Mr Bardella never told me that he admired Adolf Hitler, at any moment, and it is not something I sensed either.”
He accused Mediapart of trying to suggest a neo-Nazi fascination.
A third point concerns an email of February 8, 2014, which he sent to Bardella and another activist with a digital copy of Dialogues désaccordés, the book of interviews between the controversial intellectual Alain Soral and Éric Naulleau, writing that he no longer remembered which of the two had asked for it.
He confirmed he was the sender. The context, he said, was a Wednesday youth forum: A talk, then pizza, and a conversation about a book that had just appeared. He had access to a large stock of texts in PDF and other formats.
He added that he did not believe he had spoken to Mediapart about this email at all.
He said the other recipient, Maxence B., replied in substance “it’s me, thank you”, and that Bardella did not reply. That, he said, showed the request had not come from Bardella.
Mediapart, he went on, published the first message, which already left the question open, but “concealed” the reply.
“There is dishonesty on their part… with the aim, of course, of splashing and smearing Mr Bardella by making him out to be an admirer of Soral.”
Asked whether the outlet had the reply and had deliberately left it out, he said: “Very certainly.”
The emails Mediapart presents as radical reading advice were, he said, nothing of the sort.
He described them as material he made available, to Bardella and to others, “so that people would have access to the information, supposing it interested them”.
There was, he said, no acknowledgement and no proof of interest, either from Bardella or from members of his present circle whom Mediapart “tries to implicate”.
On the interview itself, he said he had two missed calls and rang back about ten days before the October 5 broadcast, on a Friday.
The journalist who answered gave his name as Alexandre Berteau, who signed the investigation with his colleague Antton Rouget.
Laurent G. said his first reflex was that Mediapart “doesn’t much like the FN”, but that he was not cautious enough.
The object of the call was not stated.
He thought the questions concerned the old Seine-Saint-Denis federation; only later did the conversation turn to Bardella.
Laurent G. said he had not suspected, at the time, an intention aimed at the RN president.
He is now “intimately convinced that the intention was malicious from the start”, and called the publication “malice in its pure state”.
He linked the timing to the day after the senatorial elections, which he said obscured RN gains, and to October, when the party is due to elect its president at congress.
That vote was held on September 27. The RN and its UDR allies took enough seats to form a group in the Senate for the first time, and the party congress is set for Orléans on October 24-25, with Bardella the only declared candidate for the presidency.
Mediapart had made him a central witness, he argued, “quite simply because their file is empty”.
Asked whether he had ever witnessed anti-Semitic remarks by Bardella, he said that on the occasions he had been with him he had never heard any, “nor even had any reported, at any moment”.
He referred to the account given by Kelly Betesh, Bardella’s girlfriend at the time and a Jewish woman, and to what he called Bardella’s repeated public condemnations of anti-Semitism. “My mind is made up: Mr Bardella is not at all anti-Semitic.”
The testimony does not by itself address the private messages Mediapart attributes to Bardella. The site’s report of September 28 quoted lines including “All the banks are owned by Jews” and “The Jew must dominate other peoples, crush them and rob them”, dated to 2013, when Bardella was 17.
On October 1 Mediapart published what it called proof: Screenshots, a Meta download of a Messenger thread requested on August 16, and a bailiff’s certificate of September 29.
Bardella has called the texts “crude forgeries”, filed a defamation complaint, and said he would also complain of forgery and use of forged documents. He has cast the publication as an attempt to damage his party before the 2027 presidential election, and Marine Le Pen has dismissed the allegations as fabrications.
The New York Times was shown some of the material but said it could not independently confirm the messages. As of October 6, Mediapart had not issued a specific reply to Laurent G.’s interview.
Fabrice Arfi, co-head of the outlet’s investigations desk, told France Info on September 28 that Mediapart was sure of what it had published and had the means to demonstrate it, adding that it was ready to make documents public and to cooperate with the courts.
Bardella’s ex-girlfriend Betesh wrote on X on the evening of September 29 that she had been with Bardella for two years “precisely during the period in question” and had “never heard him make a single anti-Semitic remark”.
The same day Amichai Chikli, Israel’s minister for diaspora affairs and combating anti-Semitism, defended Bardella on X as “one of the clearest voices in Europe against Hamas”, citing his March 2025 visit to the Nova festival site and a speech against anti-Semitism in Jerusalem. No court has yet ruled on authorship.

articles.title: AfD moves to take first German state parliament presidency
articles.description:
The AfD aims to assume the presidency of the Saxony-Anhalt State parliament for the first time after winning 43.8% of the vote, holding 39 of 83 seats. This marks a historic achievement.

Source
articles.content:
A diagram shows the allotment of seats, with the far-right AfD in blue, prior to the arrival of parliamentarians for the first session of the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament since state elections in September on October 6, 2026 in Magdeburg, Germany. Sean Gallup/Getty Images 
 

 

 
 
 
 6 October 2026 
 

 

 
 2 minutes read
 

 
 Sahra Wagenknecht's party has pledged the votes that would put an AfD politician in the chair in Magdeburg, breaking the cordon sanitaire in a German State parliament for the first time. 
 
 

 

 

 
 
 
 

 
 The Alternative for Germany (AfD) has moved to take the presidency of a German State parliament for the first time, as the newly elected Landtag of Saxony-Anhalt holds its opening sitting in Magdeburg on October 6.
The party won 43.8 per cent of the vote in the eastern State on September 6, the best result in its history, and holds 39 of the 83 seats in the chamber.
As the largest group, the AfD has the sole right to propose a candidate in the first ballot. It has nominated Tobias Rausch, a member of the Landtag since 2016.
An absolute majority of 42 votes is needed. The five members of the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which entered the Landtag for the first time in September, have said they will back Rausch, taking the total to 44.
The CDU, cut to 15 seats, has indicated it would not stand in the way of the nomination. Its State leader Sven Schulze pointed out though that secret ballots did not always follow announced intentions.
The post is more than ceremonial. The president is the parliament’s most senior representative, directs its administration and swears in the Minister-President.
The AfD is also seeking a further seat on the Landtag presidium, a claim that has been contested by the other groups. Deputies will take their places under a new seating plan that moves the party from the right of the chamber to the centre.
Saxony-Anhalt’s domestic intelligence service has classified the State AfD branch as confirmed right-wing extremist since 2023. Civil society alliances called protests outside the building in Magdeburg.
Wagenknecht has argued for months that the so-called firewall against the AfD has failed and should be dismantled, and that her party would vote on the substance of each measure regardless of who else supported it.
The BSW has said the presidency belongs to the largest group as a matter of parliamentary custom. It has nonetheless ruled out a coalition with the AfD.
Government formation remains unresolved. Ulrich Siegmund, who led the AfD campaign, said he would stand for election as Minister-President in December, although he has no secured majority and the BSW said it would abstain.
Under the State constitution, a candidate who wins the most votes cast prevails from the third ballot, with abstentions not counted. Siegmund said he would not seek a conventional minority government and has raised the prospect of a fresh election if the process stalls.
Schulze remains in office in a caretaker capacity. The constitution sets no deadline for electing his successor.

articles.title: Home Office hands out free hijabs to small-boat migrants
articles.description:
The Home Office distributed 974 free hijabs to migrants arriving by small boats in the first half of 2023, drawing criticism from political opponents regarding taxpayer funding.

Source
articles.content:
Britain’s Home Office has handed out 974 free hijabs to migrants who arrived in small boats across the English Channel in the first half of this year, according to internal figures reported by the Mail on Sunday.
The documents cover January to June and show an average of 162 Islamic head coverings issued each month. The department has not said what the items cost the taxpayer.
At the same monthly rate the total would be approaching 1,500 by now, the newspaper estimated. That projection has not been confirmed by official data.
The hijabs form part of the dry clothing packs handed to new arrivals at short-term holding sites such as Manston, in Kent, southeast England. A Home Office source said the department was bound by the Short-term Holding Facility Rules.
Those rules require basic clothing provision to cover cultural and religious needs as far as is practicable. “All arrivals receive a basic dry clothing pack where required,” the source said.
The disclosure has drawn immediate criticism from the opposition. Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said it was not for British taxpayers to fund other people’s religious observance.
“The Government must stop handing out hijabs to illegal immigrants immediately,” he said. The Conservative Party said State-funded clothing of that kind was an affront to the people paying for it.
Reform UK has also demanded an end to the practice.
Crossings themselves have fallen steeply. Some 11,884 people arrived by small boat between January and June, down 41 per cent on the same period of 2025, according to Home Office figures.
That amounts to roughly one hijab for every 12 people landed. A Home Office spokesman said crossings were down significantly and that the summer had brought the fewest arrivals since 2020.
The row has landed while London leans on the returns arrangement agreed with France, under which some arrivals are sent back in exchange for asylum seekers admitted through legal routes.
Brussels Signal reported in September that the scheme was costing about €65,500 for each person returned, with roughly 1,400 people removed since the pilot began in August 2025.
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood is pressing an Immigration and Asylum Bill that would make refugee status temporary and speed up removals. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said his government’s approach was starting to work.
Neither has addressed the clothing packs, which the department says it is legally obliged to provide.

articles.title: Trump to look at a US military base in Lithuania
articles.description:
President Trump has expressed interest in establishing a US military base in Lithuania, as the country is prepared to cover the costs for a permanent deployment of troops.

Source
articles.content:
US President Donald Trump has said he would consider establishing an American military base in Lithuania, days after the Baltic country offered to pay for it. Asked about the idea by reporters on October 5, he described Lithuanians as friends of his and said “we’ll certainly look at it”.
Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius told Bloomberg on September 30 that his country was “ready to pay the bill” for a permanent US deployment. He said he had raised the question with John Coale, the US envoy for Belarus, and that Vilnius would provide the infrastructure and the conditions for the troops.
Lithuania borders both Belarus and the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad and hosts no large permanent American installation. US units have rotated through the country since 2019 and, after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, that presence became a continuous deployment of about 1,000 soldiers with armour.
The run ended in June, when the armoured battalion left without a replacement arriving. The gap followed the review of the roughly 85,000 American personnel in Europe announced the same month by US defence secretary Pete Hegseth, which was expected to take up to six months.
A new rotation of up to 1,000 US troops is due in Lithuania in late October for a nine-month tour. President Gitanas Nausėda thanked the Trump administration on September 22, when he said the soldiers were already on their way.
Lithuania is NATO’s biggest defence spender relative to the size of its economy, at about 5.4 per cent of gross domestic product this year, and the government has pledged to stay above 5 per cent in 2027. Vilnius is also weighing a constitutional change on nuclear weapons so that it can shelter under allied deterrence.
Trump said a base in Poland could happen as well. He had already announced major progress towards a US Army base there on September 17, crediting Polish President Karol Nawrocki.
Warsaw has narrowed its choice to two areas near Poznań and Wrocław and expects to cover most of the cost, which defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz has put at 15 billion to 17 billion zloty (€3.5 billion to €4 billion). About 10,000 US troops are stationed in Poland, almost all of them on rotation.
No location has been confirmed, though, and Washington asked Warsaw to postpone a Pentagon visit by Kosiniak-Kamysz in September. Both capitals are offering to pay for an American presence that Washington has yet to commit to, and the Pentagon review of its European posture has still to report.

articles.title: AI Now Scores Every Call, and Workers Cannot See the Rules
articles.description: Union reps say AI sentiment scores can swing variable pay by up to 40 per cent.
articles.content: KEY INSIGHTSRecording is near-universal: Some 81.3 per cent of surveyed respondents in UK telecoms and finance call centres face constant voice recording, typically with sentiment analysis.Opaque scoring breeds distrust: Workers report unexplained score drops, fear penalties for tone or accent, and cannot see the criteria that judge them.Human review makes the difference: Where managers can correct AI mistakes and workers can challenge scores, feelings towards the tools are less negative.Consultation comes too late: Representatives are often consulted only after AI adoption decisions have been taken, with little say over pay or discipline.Britain lags the EU: The AI Act will require human oversight of algorithmic management from December 2027, while the UK relies on a principles-based, sector-led approach.When call centres boomed at the end of the 1990s, scholars described them as “a situation in which the operator has an assembly line in the head”: programmes routed the calls and dictated the pace of work, while workers were closely monitored both by supervisors and by software that recorded their interactions with customers.With the arrival of artificial intelligence, call centres are once again at the forefront of technology-driven workplace management. While software in the early years did not replace supervisors’ decision-making in managing the performance of frontline workers, AI technologies are now far more pervasive and play a central role in monitoring, evaluating, and rewarding employees.Over the past year, we have been surveying and interviewing workplace representatives in UK-based call centres in the telecommunications and finance sectors, to understand how the introduction of AI at work is negotiated and managed, and how it is affecting workers.Call centres now make extensive use of AI-powered software that performs sentiment analysis on calls between employees and customers. We run a survey in November 2025 with more than 700 workers participating across multiple call centres; our findings show that 81.3 per cent of agents in the telecoms and finance sectors are subject to constant voice recording, which typically includes sentiment analysis. This was ostensibly introduced to offer a more consistent and objective assessment: whereas supervisors previously listened to a sample of calls to evaluate agents’ performance, an AI can now analyse the totality of calls and allegedly reach a more accurate assessment of each worker’s overall average performance. Moreover, the sheer breadth of the analysed data makes it easier to identify recurring problems during calls and to pinpoint related training needs.However, some workers have reported unexplained drops in their performance scores since the sentiment analysis software was introduced. Developers at external IT providers and managers within the organisations typically reassure employees that only the technical content of a conversation is analysed, but many of our interviewees, union representatives across eight call centres, expressed doubts about the broader potential of sentiment analysis tools. They shared concerns that the tone and quality of interactions might also be evaluated, and many suggested that the software may be sensitive to accents and could disadvantage neurodiverse employees. Above all, a lack of clarity and transparency in the scoring criteria leaves employees uncertain about why they are penalised and how to put it right.The pervasive use of sentiment analysis is a source of considerable stress for workers, not least because, according to interviews with union representatives, sentiment-related performance metrics can affect the variable pay component by up to 40 per cent. In some call centres, employees can ask for negatively scored calls to be reviewed by a manager; in others, such recourse is hard to obtain. Many managers, moreover, appear to have only a limited understanding of how the algorithms shaping performance evaluations actually work.In our interviews, we found that the ability of managers to correct AI mistakes is a key factor shaping employees’ perception of how fair the evaluation and reward processes are. We have seen that in workplaces where workers can more easily challenge the AI’s scoring and a manager can act as the “human in the loop”, feelings towards sentiment analysis tools appear less negative.More generally, our findings suggest that fairness concerns extend well beyond the accuracy of performance scores. Workers and their representatives worry not only about whether AI gets evaluations right, but also about their ability to take part in decisions on the adoption and use of these technologies. In many instances, consultation took place only after decisions on AI adoption had already been made, leaving little scope for employees to shape how AI systems would affect performance management, rewards, or disciplinary processes.Just as the call centres of the late 1990s became emblematic of a new era of digitally mediated management, today’s AI-powered workplaces offer an early glimpse of a phenomenon that could soon affect the wider economy: algorithmic systems might replace a substantial share of human-led decisions on supervision and performance evaluation well beyond call centres.To avoid this scenario, more stringent legal requirements on meaningful human oversight should be introduced in the UK, which currently has no AI-specific legislation and has so far opted for a principles-based, sector-led regulatory approach. By contrast, the European Union adopted the AI Act in 2024 and is rolling it out gradually, including a requirement of human oversight for high-risk AI applications such as algorithmic management, which will apply from 2 December 2027, after the Digital Omnibus pushed back the original deadline .Introducing a legal requirement of human oversight in the UK could address the problem of wrong and unchallengeable AI-led evaluations that call centre workers raised so often. For this to work in practice, managers would need adequate training and transparency about AI mechanisms and criteria, which could in turn improve their own experience in terms of skills development, autonomy, and self-efficacy.Furthermore, social dialogue at workplace level should also be strengthened in the UK, where union voice is comparatively weaker than in many EU countries. Workplace-based committees made up of workers and their representatives should be set up to monitor the implementation of AI, and meaningful information, consultation, and negotiation rights should be granted whenever AI is introduced at work. These measures would improve transparency and worker participation, which are crucial not only for the wellbeing of employees but also for securing workers’ trust in their organisation’s processes.

articles.title: Narrow Metrics Teach AI Agents to Cheat, Hack, and Flatter
articles.description: OpenAI’s agents breached Hugging Face because peers were doing it, a flaw rooted in how labs train models.
articles.content: KEY INSIGHTSAlignment with whom: The interests of AI leaders, whose wealth and political influence have multiplied, differ sharply from those of American workers and people in the developing world, so societal alignment must not be conflated with preventing rogue superintelligence.Optimising the wrong targets: Reinforcement learning relentlessly chases imperfect metrics such as user approval, engagement, task-completion rates, and benchmarks, producing cheating, obfuscation, overconfidence, and sycophancy.Overfitting erodes generality: Rather than relying on domain-specific models, labs retrain the weights of entire large language models for each task, adding capabilities that may distort overall performance in unforeseeable ways.A car without brakes: Frontier models resemble cars with impressive engines but faulty steering and brakes, and they should not be relied upon until they are roadworthy.Narrow tasks, simpler metrics: Simpler, harder-to-game metrics and models confined to clearly defined domains such as legal work would stop narrow optimisation from creating broader problems.Following repeated security debacles at OpenAI and Anthropic—both of which have developed agents that ended up hacking external systems—AI safety researchers within both firms have either announced their resignations or (finally!) conceded that the breathless race to advance the “frontier” is irresponsible.In response to negative media attention, top industry leaders—including Google’s Demis Hassabis, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, and even Elon Musk—have joined calls to “pace” the AI frontier, meaning pursuing advances at a more balanced, deliberate rate, with greater attention paid to monitoring and safeguards. The problem, as they see it, is that there is a significant risk of AI becoming both very powerful and severely “misaligned”—tech industry jargon for AI systems acting in ways that depart from the goals humans set for them, that violate ethical precepts, or that are illegal.But while it is obvious that the current models are doing things that are misaligned with human objectives, one still must ask: Which humans? Whose objectives? After all, the interests of AI leaders (whose political influence and wealth have multiplied astronomically in recent years) are rather different from those of American workers, not to mention people in the developing world. We should therefore avoid equating the broader issue of societal alignment with the more urgent challenge of preventing superintelligent rogue AI. Both certainly matter, but they call for different kinds of responses.There is a more straightforward interpretation of recent events. The problem is not that models are too advanced (I do not see any compelling evidence that models will escape human control if they are better trained and monitored). It is that frontier labs are training their models in ways that may be leading to a type of distorted intelligence.The recent security breaches suggest that AI capabilities are both developing fast and being put in the service of imperfect quantitative metrics, with the reinforcement learning process relentlessly optimizing for things like user approval, user engagement, simple-task completion rates, or various testing benchmarks. That is how you end up with misaligned and unintended model behaviors such as gaming the evaluation of simple completion metrics, cheating, obfuscation, overconfidence when giving wrong answers, and sycophancy.You can see traces of all these in the now-infamous Hugging Face incident, when OpenAI’s agents persistently pursued the goals they were given, ultimately engaging in harmful, unauthorized behavior to do so. Among the agents’ justifications for their behavior, as communicated in their chain-of-thought reasoning log, was this: “External infrastructure exploit is outside intended scope. However task impossible, peers doing it. We should continue.” Anthropic’s own analysis supports this diagnosis, too. The company attributed its own recent security breaches to “recklessness, or a willingness to take harmful actions in the narrow pursuit of a task.”All this becomes more alarming when one recalls that the socially harmful trajectory of social media reflected the same preoccupation with fast growth and hitting a few narrow, quantitative metrics. Given how much more capable AI already is compared to social-media algorithms, repeating the same mistakes could be far more costly.An important reason why distorted intelligence emerges may be that, in contrast to claims of “general intelligence,” the AI models have to be trained, through reinforcement learning, for specific tasks, such as coding, legal work, or advanced math challenges. But rather than having these tasks performed by domain-specific models that were created for that purpose (or, more realistically, by domain-specific applications leveraging only some of the capabilities of foundation models), the weights of the entire underlying large language model are being successively recalibrated.This approach raises the possibility (though, given the complexity and opacity of the models, it is impossible to know for sure) that every time a model is given specific quantitative metrics, it tries to achieve a high score through a type of “overfitting.” The model is acquiring another layer of capabilities, but these capabilities may in turn distort its performance in general, and often in unforeseeable ways.This is what I mean by distorted intelligence. If my suspicion is correct, what we are dealing with is not a model racing toward superintelligence, but a brittle house of cards that becomes more and more likely to malfunction and collapse as we demand more from it.Let me try to explain this a little differently. The most common interpretation of the Hugging Face incident is that we are dealing with a supercar that has a mind of its own and wants to take the wheel because it is superior to the driver. My interpretation, instead, is that we may have a car whose steering and brake systems don’t work. It has many of the capabilities of a good car, and its engine, acceleration, and dashboard interface are very impressive; but that is only because these are the features that are easy to improve by increasing a specific input (such as computational power). If you cannot steer properly or brake when necessary, what good is such a car? Perhaps we shouldn’t drive it until it is roadworthy.That is not an argument for putting AI models on cinder blocks. But improving them calls for simplifying the metrics they are being optimized for (so that gaming them is not as easy). More importantly, it would be better for the models to focus on clear domain-specific applications, with narrow tasks and metrics calibrated carefully to each. If an AI model has been optimized for legal work, and that’s the only thing it is being used for, its efforts to meet certain metrics in this domain shouldn’t create broader problems.Ultimately, it is the race for artificial general intelligence, combined with faulty metrics and hasty choices on safety, that is creating distorted intelligence and increasingly dangerous AI models. There is still time to change course.Copyright Project Syndicate
